text.p: ITT Hartford Group Inc significantly boosted reserves for asbestos and environmental losses on Friday in a move that will eliminate a major drag on future earnings.
The move, which had been expected, is the second major addition to reserves for asbestos and environmental liabilities in four years.
In 1992, ITT Hartford added $594 million after-tax to asbestos and environmental reserves and another $165 million after-tax for expected legal defense costs.
The latest reserve addition was expected to resolve Hartford's environmental liability for the forseeable future, analysts said.
"This puts it behind them for the time being," said Standard & Poor's analyst Jonathan Godown.
ITT Hartford said it will boost reserves for asbestos and environmental liabilities to $2.15 billion from $1.3 billion with an after-tax charge of $510 million.
Lehman analyst Peter Wade said the charge was larger than he expected, but should make it one of the best reserved companies in the industry.
"Investors should be comfortable that the company won't be back to the trough for any reserve charges in the forseeable future," Wade said.
But potential losses from catastrophes will keep earnings volatile and could put the insurer under increasing pressure to take steps to reduce exposure to catastrophes, Wade said.

"The market is going to be less and less forgiving about it in future years," Wade said. As a result, he said, he believes Hartford will have to consider steps to reduce the earnings volatility, just as other major insurers have done in recent months.
Nationwide Insurance earlier this month said it will reduce sales of new property insurance policies in the coastal counties of 17 states to reduce its exposure to major catastrophes.
And Allstate Corp has taken a series of steps over the last year to reduce exposure to earthquakes in California and hurricanes on the East Coast.
But Standard & Poor's Godown said ITT Hartford's catastrophe exposure was not a major concern for the rating agency.
"I was fairly impressed with their catastrophe management program," he said. Godown also noted that any drastic sales reduction in states like Florida could hurt the company's business with retirees.
ITT Hartford reported a third quarter loss on Friday of $4.63 a share after $693 million in non-recurring, after-tax charges. That compares to a $1.48 a share profit a year ago.
Catastrophe claims for the period were unusually high at $49 million, more than triple the $14 million reported a year ago.
Excluding the charges, The Hartford would have reported $150 million of net income for the quarter, down 13 percent from a year ago.
Core earnings were $132 million, down 15 percent from $155 million a year ago, primarily due to the high catastrophe claims and the resolution of several large environmental cases.
The earnings, excluding the one-time charges, were about in line with expectations, Wade said.
With the special non-recurring items out of the way, ITT Hartford must now show the ability to generate good earnings growth and good returns in an increasingly competitive industry.
"I think those issues are the ones that face the company in 1997," Wade said. "That's the challenge that lays in front of them."
